text: This lesson writes the actual code for quantumlib's three modules against last lesson's requirements, applying the architecture pattern from Chapter 3 and the testing discipline from Chapter 2 together, for real, on all three algorithms at once.

This lesson covers implementing all three capstone modules following the backend-abstraction pattern, writing the matching tiered test suite for each one, implementing the resource-estimation functions as real, tested code rather than one-off scratch calculations, and verifying the Grover iteration-count formula against the known value from Lesson 19.

The Bell and GHZ module builds the circuit with a guard against fewer than two qubits, a Hadamard, a chain of CX gates, and a measurement. Its test file carries the full tiering from Chapter 2: construction tests parametrized across sizes, a statevector test confirming exact structure, and a statistical test asserting the z-score is within the ninety-nine percent confidence threshold.

The Grover module's resource-estimation function implements the exact iteration-count formula, and its test isn't a throwaway sanity check — it asserts the function returns 25 for 1024 items, the exact numeric claim verified back in Lesson 19, now locked into the test suite so a future refactor of this function can't silently drift from the verified value.

The QAOA module's run function takes the backend as a parameter, never importing a concrete backend class directly — satisfying Lesson 11's requirement. Its shot-budget estimator implements the parameter-shift-rule formula as real code, and its test asserts the function matches Lesson 19's worked example exactly: three layers, 100 iterations, 2000 shots per evaluation, giving 2.4 million total shots.

Each module maps directly onto last lesson's requirements: construction tests parametrized across sizes, a statevector check, a statistical test with a documented confidence level, a tested resource-estimation function matching the exact verified formula, and backend injection via the shared interface rather than a hardcoded import. Next lesson closes the gap this one deliberately deferred: documentation and worked examples.
